title: What an AI Chatbot Is, and Is Not
intro: Find out what an AI chatbot really does, what it is good for, and why it can sound sure while being wrong.
recap: A chatbot writes the words that are most likely to come next. It does not know things the way a person does.
It is good for drafting, explaining, summarising and brainstorming.
It can invent names, numbers and sources. This is called a hallucination.
Use it for what it does well, and check the rest.

aiTutor.recap: An AI chatbot writes the most likely next words. It is useful, but it is not a person and not a search of facts. Keep that picture in mind and the rest of the course makes sense.
aiTutor.example: Ask a chatbot for the capital of a country and it will usually be right, because that fact appears in text everywhere. Ask it for a small town's population last year and it may give a precise number that is simply made up.
aiTutor.watchOut: Smooth writing feels like intelligence, so it is easy to trust. A chatbot writes a wrong answer in the same polished voice as a right one.
aiTutor.tryThis: Next time you use your phone's word suggestions, notice how it guesses the next word. A chatbot does the same, only far better.

glossary.definition: A program you chat with in plain language. An AI chatbot was trained on huge amounts of text, and it writes its replies word by word.
glossary.example: Typing "Explain how a bank loan works in simple words" and getting a short explanation back is a chatbot at work.

glossary.definition: When an AI states something false or made-up in a confident, believable way. It is not lying on purpose; it is writing what sounds likely.
glossary.example: A chatbot names a book and an author that do not exist, with a believable title and year.

glossary.definition: Coming up with many ideas quickly, without judging them yet. Chatbots are good at it because ideas do not have to be exactly right.
glossary.example: Asking for ten possible names for a small tailoring shop and picking the ones you like.

paragraphs: Think of the way your phone suggests the next word while you type. An AI chatbot does something like that, but on a much larger scale. It looks at your question and writes the words that are most likely to come next.
That makes it very good at drafting, explaining, summarising and brainstorming. It also means it does not "know" things the way a person does, and it does not check facts as it writes.
So it can sound completely sure while being wrong. People call this a hallucination. The skill in this course is to use the tool for what it does well, and to check the rest.

aiTutor.explain: Think about how the chatbot decides what to write. It picks likely words, and nothing in that process checks whether the result is true. So a confident voice tells you about its style, not about the facts.
aiTutor.watchOut: Long and detailed answers look more trustworthy, but extra detail only gives a wrong answer more places to be wrong.

widgetData.question: A chatbot gives a long, confident answer. What does the confident tone tell you about whether it is correct?

options.text: Nothing. It writes in a confident style even when it is wrong.
It must be correct, because it sounds so sure.
It is correct if the answer is long enough.

widgetData.explanation: The tool is built to write fluent, believable text. Fluent text can still contain wrong facts, so tone and length are not proof of correctness.
widgetData.bonusFact: A wrong answer and a right answer can look equally polished. That is why the habit of checking matters more than a feeling of being convinced.

aiTutor.explain: Decide whether each statement is true or false. Ask yourself whether the task is about language, where a rough draft helps, or about exact facts, where being wrong can hurt.
aiTutor.tryThis: For each card, think of one real job in your own life that fits it.

widgetData.instruction: Is each statement true or false?

cards.statement: A chatbot is a good helper for drafting a message, summarising a text or listing ideas.
cards.explanation: These are tasks about language, where a rough first version helps and you can easily judge the result.
cards.bonusFact: Treat the result as a first draft that you edit, not a finished piece.

cards.statement: A chatbot always looks up the latest facts before it answers.
cards.explanation: Many chatbots work from what they learned earlier, and may miss recent events unless the tool says it can search.
cards.bonusFact: If your question depends on today's news or prices, check a current source.

cards.statement: A chatbot can make up names, numbers and sources that do not exist.
cards.explanation: It writes what sounds likely, so it can invent details that look real.
cards.bonusFact: Names, numbers and web links need extra care, because they must be exactly right.

cards.statement: A chatbot understands you the way a close friend does.
cards.explanation: It works with patterns in text. It does not know you or your situation unless you tell it.
cards.bonusFact: Tell it what you need and who it is for, but leave out private details.

screens.title: Match the Task to the Right Level of Trust

aiTutor.review: Match each task to how much checking it needs. The rule is simple: the more a wrong answer could cost you, the more you check it somewhere else.
aiTutor.example: A name for a shop is your own taste. A date on a legal document must be exactly right, so you confirm it from the official source.
aiTutor.watchOut: A task can look harmless but still carry risk. A quote, a number or a medicine dose is a fact, even if it sits inside a casual chat.

widgetData.instruction: Match each task to how much checking it needs:

pairs.left: Brainstorm names for a small shop
pairs.right: Light check: your own taste decides

pairs.left: Explain a topic in simple words
pairs.right: Medium check: compare with a trusted source

pairs.left: State a date, a number or a quote
Advice on health, law or money

widgetData.explanation: The more a wrong answer could cost you, the more you should check it somewhere else.

aiTutor.review: Finish the sentence about your role when you use a chatbot. The tool drafts quickly, but you are the one who answers for the result.
aiTutor.tryThis: Before the next lesson, think of one thing you could ask a chatbot to draft this week, and what you would check before using it.

widgetData.template: A chatbot is a helper, and you are still the one who must {blank} the answer.
widgetData.explanation: The tool can draft quickly, but it does not take responsibility. Judging the result is your job, because only you know what is true and what is at stake.
widgetData.bonusFact: The next lessons show how to ask better questions and how to check what comes back. Together they turn a quick guesser into a useful helper.
